entities.evidence: The verse identifies Ham as Canaan’s father, matching the son of Noah.
The phrase אֲבִי כְנַעַן identifies Canaan as Ham’s son.

review.translation: [Then|0] [Ham|1], [the father of|2] [Canaan|3], [saw|0] [the nakedness of|5,4] [his father|6], [and he told|7] [his|9] [two|8] [brothers|9] [outside|10].

analysis.evidence: חָם is the subject, and אֵת marks עֶרְוַת אָבִיו (“his father’s nakedness”) as the direct object. The phrase identifies what Ham saw with his eyes.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed conjunction וַ־.

draft.change: Retain the current personal-name article. Its Genesis 9:18 note already explains the repeated name.
draft.definition: Ham, son of Noah and father of Canaan.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 9:18, הוּא refers back to the repeated חָם and אֲבִי כְנָעַן identifies him as Canaan’s father.

analysis.evidence: חָם names the man who saw his father’s nakedness. The phrase אֲבִי כְנַעַן immediately follows his name and identifies him as Canaan’s father.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It is the subject of וַיַּרְא.
analysis.sense: Ham, son of Noah and father of Canaan

analysis.evidence: In חָם אֲבִי כְנַעַן, the phrase אֲבִי כְנַעַן identifies Ham as Canaan’s father.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state, with כְנַעַן as its complement.

analysis.evidence: The verse identifies Ham as חָם אֲבִי כְנַעַן, “Ham, the father of Canaan.” The kinship term אֲבִי identifies Canaan as Ham’s son.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It completes the construct phrase אֲבִי כְנַעַן, “father of Canaan.”

analysis.evidence: אֵת introduces עֶרְוַת אָבִיו, “his father’s nakedness,” as the direct object of וַיַּרְא, “he saw.” The possessive suffix on אָבִיו makes the construct phrase definite.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וַיַּרְא חָם ... אֵת עֶרְוַת אָבִיו, “Ham saw his father’s nakedness,” אֵת marks the construct phrase עֶרְוַת אָבִיו as the object of “saw.”
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in the construct state. Its absolute ending ־ָה appears as ־ַת before אָבִיו, “his father.”

analysis.evidence: Ham sees עֶרְוַת אָבִיו, “the nakedness of his father.” The suffix identifies Noah as Ham’s father.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Ham.

analysis.evidence: Ham saw his father’s nakedness and then told his two brothers outside. לִשְׁנֵי אֶחָיו identifies the recipients, and the preceding clause supplies what he told them.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וַ introduces a Hiphil wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular. Its subject is Ham.
analysis.sense: tell someone that something is the case

analysis.evidence: In לִשְׁנֵי אֶחָיו ‘to his two brothers’, שְׁנֵי gives the number of brothers whom Ham told.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לִ־ marks the recipient of וַיַּגֵּד ‘he told’. שְׁנֵי is the masculine dual construct form of the cardinal numeral שְׁנַיִם.

analysis.evidence: Ham sees his father’s nakedness and tells לִשְׁנֵי אֶחָיו, “his two brothers.” The family context supports the literal sibling sense.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural construct noun with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Ham.

analysis.evidence: Ham told his two brothers בַּחוּץ. The phrase locates the telling outside the tent where his father lay.
analysis.morphology: The prefix בַּ combines the preposition בְּ with the definite article. חוּץ is a masculine singular noun in the absolute state. The phrase functions adverbially.
